title: The Influence of Provaping "Gatewatchers" on the Dissemination of COVID-19 Misinformation on Twitter: Analysis of Twitter Discourse Regarding Nicotine and the COVID-19 Pandemic
screen_reason: Content analysis of 1,420,271 tobacco-and-COVID-19 tweets (January-September 2020) reporting several shares with explicit denominators: 22.5% of the 253 most-shared URLs and 10.7% of the 1000 most-retweeted posts carried the claim that nicotine, tobacco or vaping treats or prevents COVID-19; those posts drew 3.8% of retweets in the top-1000 sample; 55.8% of the 163 top users retweeted at least one such post; and the top 0.12% of users accounted for 10.93% of all content.

estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL, hence borderline=true: this is the only pair in the paper that satisfies R1 (both the group share of users, 0.12%, and their share of activity, 10.93%, are stated verbatim in one sentence), but the 10.93% is a share of ALL tobacco-and-COVID content, not of misinformation content. If the review's CONCENTRATION construct requires the concentrated quantity to be misinformation, this row should be dropped. The one sentence that states both halves of the pair is split across the PDF's two columns in the text file, so source_quote carries the 10.93% activity share and moderator_quote the 0.12% user share; in the printed paper they are one sentence.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted, with reasons. (1) 'Only 25 (2.5%) users posted 3 or more SDs from the median number of posts, meaning 2.49% of all activity came from the top 25 users' - the 2.5% is a share of the top-1000 list, not of the 817,691 users, so pairing it with the 2.49% activity share would mis-state the concentration; the correct group share (25/817,691) is not stated and I may not compute it. Same problem for the 163 top users responsible for 5.59% of all content: the activity share is given but the user share is not, so R1 fails. (2) 'Among these top 29 URLs, 12 URLs linked articles promoting the potential therapeutic value of nicotine, vaping, or tobacco against COVID-19, accounting for 41.4% of shares among this top content' - 12/29 is exactly 41.4%, so the sentence appears to label a URL-count share as a share of shares; the Discussion then describes the same quantity as 'nearly 1 in 3 shares'. The three descriptions cannot all be right, and the 253-URL row above covers the same measure on a cleaner denominator. (3) Vape-advocate prevalence among top users (49.7% of the top 163, 88% of the top 25) is a share of accounts holding an advocacy stance, not a misinformation share. (4) The vape-advocate vs other-top-user split of the actor-share row (63% vs 40.3% retweeting at least one such post) is the paper's headline comparison and could justify two subgroup rows; I kept only the overall 55.8% to avoid triple-counting a curated denominator, and record the split here so an adjudicator can add it. (5) Retweet-proportion figures (78.6% of vape advocates' posts vs 53.1% of others' were retweets), hashtag volumes (vaping hashtags 9.4% of all hashtags), bot scores, and '38.2% of top posts were retweeted at least once by top users' are not misinformation shares. (6) 'the therapeutic nicotine claim to be prevalent in about 1% of tweets relevant to both the pandemic and tobacco' and 'Pew estimates that 97% of tweets are produced by the top 25% of users' are figures cited from Kavuluru et al. and Pew respectively, which R8 forbids keeping. (7) Country is genuinely unassignable: the corpus is not geolocated and the most-shared URLs are South African, French, British, American and Indian. NOTE ON QUOTES: this text file interleaves the PDF's two print columns line by line, so no sentence longer than one printed line exists as a contiguous span; every quote is therefore truncated at a column line break rather than at a sentence boundary.

rob.design: Near-census content analysis of Twitter. NORC's tobacco archive was collected monthly through the Historical Powertrack API and sorted by a naive Bayes relevance classifier; a keyword filter for COVID-19 content was developed and validated against 2566 human-coded original tweets (precision 0.90, recall 0.89, F1 0.89), producing 1,420,271 posts from 817,691 users and 54,806 URLs for January-September 2020. Analytic sets are rank-truncated at inflection points (top 1000 users, top 163 users, top 253 URLs, top 1000 retweets, top 1000 hashtags). The top-1000 retweet content analysis used two independent coders on a grounded-theory scheme; 300 posts (30%) were double-coded, with Cohen kappa = 1.00 for the protective-role-of-nicotine category and 0.80-0.95 for the other five. Bot exposure assessed with Botometer (mean 1.59, SD 1.37). Authors flag that private and removed accounts mean some content was missed, and that they analysed a small fraction of the full corpus.
